planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root tree in spring in deep, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; give the young tree light shade for its first season, then move it into full sun as it matures.

directions: Rappahannock is one of Neal Peterson's seven named Peterson Pawpaw selections and is notable for ripening earlier than its siblings, typically in mid-September, which spreads the harvest window and gets fruit off the tree before early fall storms. The flesh is a brighter yellow than most pawpaws, low in fiber, and unusually low in seed count for the genus, making it a favorite for fresh eating. Like all pawpaws it is self-incompatible, so a second, genetically distinct cultivar or seedling must be planted nearby for pollination and fruit set. Expect grafted trees to begin bearing in four to six years, with best performance where winters deliver reliable chilling but summers stay long and warm.

common_name: IXL Pawpaw (Large Late-Season Davis x Overleese Pawpaw)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root tree in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil; site in a spot that gets afternoon shade the first year, then full sun thereafter.

directions: IXL is a historic named pawpaw resulting from a cross of two other well-regarded selections, Davis and Overleese, and it combines their traits into a tree that produces some of the largest fruit in the genus with a notably late ripening date, extending the pawpaw season into October in most climates. Because pawpaws are self-incompatible, plant IXL within about 20 feet of a second unrelated cultivar to ensure reliable cross-pollination and heavy fruit set. Give young trees part shade and consistent moisture for their first year or two, then transition them to full sun as they establish a deep taproot. The large, custard-textured fruit is best harvested when it begins to soften and give slightly at the stem end.

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root tree in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; shade the trunk and root zone the first year to prevent leaf scorch while the tree establishes.

directions: Convis was selected from the same Michigan fields kept by fruit collector Corwin Davis that produced the well-known 'Davis' pawpaw, and it stands out for very large fruit that can approach a pound each, with rich yellow flesh and a mild, sweet flavor. As with all pawpaws, it is self-incompatible and needs a genetically distinct second cultivar planted nearby to set a full crop. It prefers deep, fertile, evenly moist soil and benefits from partial shade while young before converting to full sun as a mature tree. Harvest when the fruit yields to gentle pressure and separates easily from the branch, usually over several weeks in early to mid fall.

common_name: Darrow Che (Seedless Self-Fertile Mandarin Melon Berry)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or rooted-cutting tree in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Darrow tolerates poor, dry, or alkaline soils far better than most fruiting trees and needs little fuss once established.

directions: Che is a close relative of mulberry and Osage orange grown for its mulberry-shaped, maroon-red fruit that tastes something like a cross between fig and watermelon; the species is normally dioecious, but Darrow is a female selection propagated from a tree grown by USDA breeder George Darrow that reliably sets a full, seedless crop with no male pollinator required. It carries essentially no winter chilling requirement, so it flowers and fruits without the cold-dormancy failures that limit many temperate fruits in mild Gulf Coast winters, while the tree itself tolerates temperatures well below what its heat tolerance would suggest. Expect a large shrub or small tree that can be kept compact with annual pruning; young wood is thorny, so training to an open, easily harvested form early pays off later. Fruit ripens over an extended late-summer to fall window and is best picked when fully soft.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Great Wall Persimmon (Hardy Astringent Asian Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Great Wall is self-fruitful and does not need a second tree for pollination.

directions: Great Wall got its name when plant geographer J. Russell Smith spotted a superior tree growing near the Great Wall of China in the 1920s and brought scionwood back to the United States, and it remains one of the hardiest and most productive astringent-type Asian persimmons available. The medium-sized, squarish fruit is firm and puckery until fully soft, at which point the flesh turns a rich cinnamon-orange and sweet with none of the astringency remaining, so plan to let it ripen on a windowsill or in the fridge until it gives completely to gentle pressure. The tree stays compact at around 20 feet, is upright and long-lived, bears heavily once established, and colors up with strong red fall foliage that makes it a genuine landscape asset as well as a fruit tree. It tolerates a wider range of soils than most fruiting trees but still performs best with good drainage and full sun.

common_name: Gulfsnow Peach (Low-Chill White-Fleshed Gulf Series Peach)

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or grafted tree in late winter while dormant, in full sun with excellent drainage; Gulfsnow needs only about 400 chill hours, well within reach of most zone 8-9 Gulf South winters.

directions: Gulfsnow was developed through a joint USDA Agricultural Research Service, University of Georgia, and University of Florida breeding effort as part of the low-chill Gulf series of peaches, sized for growers whose winters are too mild for standard commercial varieties. It carries firm, non-melting, white flesh under skin that blushes red over a pale ground color, and it ripens in early June at trial sites in the Deep South, cropping more reliably from year to year than older low-chill selections. Being self-fertile, a single tree will set a full crop, though thinning young fruit to about 6 inches apart along the branch improves final size and quality. Its non-melting flesh holds up unusually well for fresh eating and processing compared to most low-chill peaches, which tend to soften quickly after ripening.
sources: University of Georgia College of Agricultural & Environmental Sciences
